2018-4-1.examiner_comment: The students did extremely well on these questions, with a median mark of 17 out of 20. As far as I can tell, the questions were of similar difficulty as earlier years, which seems to suggest that the move to a Prolog-style teaching methodology, where the lectures are pre-recorded and the lecture time converted to lab time, is a success. As a result I plan on introducing some more difficult components to next year's exam.

topics: Linked Lists and Data Structures in C

2018-4-3.examiner_comment: Setting this question was something of an experiment. It is mostly book work, but since compilers covers a very wide range of topics I expected students to be weak in some areas and stronger in others. This turned out not to be the case. They all seem to know their book work!

2018-4-4.examiner_comment: When I set this question I thought it was far too easy. However, only 12 attempted and the median was low (10.5). This shows once again that it is hard for me to judge what the students consider easy or hard.

2018-4-8.examiner_comment: This question had a fairly large bookwork component: (a) defining free variables and capture-avoiding substitution, (b) defining left-to-right CBV reduction, and (e) a simple inductive proof. Many candidates dealt well with all of these, though too many didn't get the capture-avoidance condition correct, and a few didn't attempt to give mathematical definitions. Then (c, d) it had an unusual environment semantics; most were able to evaluate an example and identify what would happen in a deliberately broken variation. A number of candidates visibly ran out of time. 92 attempts, mean 14.1.

2018-4-9.examiner_comment: Of the candidates that attempted this, most did well (18 attempts, mean 15.5), especially on the first part. I put this down to self-selection, with this being the second of two Semantics questions in their own section, and the one requiring more thinking and less bookwork.

2018-5-4.examiner_comment: Students overall responded well to the questions. Most deducted marks come from sub questions (b) (ii) and (c) (iv).

2018-5-5.examiner_comment: Students responded well to most of the questions. In (b) most students described the two protocols and commented on the aspects asked but did not actually compare as asked by the question. Question (c) (iv) was answered correctly by a subset of students.

2018-5-6.examiner_comment: Students responded well to most of the questions. The most challenging question was (c).

2018-5-7.examiner_comment: 28 scripts were submitted, a relatively small number, with a median mark of 10.5 and substantial spread across the mark range. (a) and (b) were generally well answered. Most students correctly concluded that (c) involved a deadlock, realising that the idea also applied to blocking primitives other than locks, but lost marks due to unclear event sequences or explanations. Some students scored quite well on (d), on realising that ideas about priority inheritance can also be applied to producer-consumer queues, but no students achieved full marks due to gaps in their solutions for example, many students failed to describe priority de-escalation following a successful read or write, losing substantial marks.

2018-5-8.examiner_comment: 43 scripts were submitted, with a median mark of 14 with a relatively tight clustering around that mark. The first half of the question, (a), (b), (c), (d), and (e), were generally well answered, leading to few marks lost for the majority of students, reflecting a good overall factual knowledge of the Bully Algorithm. The majority of lost marks were in the more complex final two sections of the question, (f) and (g), which require careful reasoning about the behaviour of the algorithm in the presence of failures. In (f), many candidates failed to consider network changes, such as link failure and recovery relating to partitions, as potential sources of disruption to election results. In (g), most students failed to clearly describe the atomicity requirements during recovery, or did not consider the potential role of persistence in ensuring that transaction IDs were not reused following failures of more substantial numbers of nodes.

2018-6-1.examiner_comment: This was mostly rather poorly answered. In section (a) there was often evidence of confusion of the difference between propositional and predicate logic, with candidates giving answers involving, for example, unusual mixtures of the two, or mixing situation calculus with a SAT encoding. In part (b) many did not address the fact that it is the underlying SAT problem that needs to be solved. Instead, they described a local search on the planning problem directly. Some answered an entirely different question, for example by talking about A-star search, or planning problems in general.

2018-6-2.examiner_comment: Section (a) was often answered semi-correctly, but many lost marks through simple omissions, such as not mentioning the need for forward propagation. Many also seemed to miss the fact that this is backpropagation as presented in the lectures, and therefore did not compute $\delta$ explicitly, although some nonetheless reached a correct solution. Some candidates described gradient descent, which was not asked for. Section (b) was much less well answered. Many correctly noticed that the output layer is unchanged. Most dealt with the modifications for the hidden layer poorly, although there was a small number of very good answers.

2018-6-3.examiner_comment: A large number of attempts, and a good median mark, suggesting that this is something the candidates understood. The first 8 marks were definitions and examples. While full marks required accurate statements, generous partial credit was given for small variations from the precise definition. Parts (c) and (d) required demonstrating understanding of the definitions, and many different solutions were possible. Only a couple of candidates got full marks in part (d).

2018-6-4.examiner_comment: This question attracted fewer attempts than the other question in complexity theory. This is possibly because the topic (on space complexity) was covered towards the end of the lecture course and may not have been revised by as many students. The overall performance was good, with a reasonable number of students showing a sound understanding of space-bounded reductions.

2018-6-5.examiner_comment: A high number of attempts, and a median mark somewhat on the low side. The marks were fairly normally distributed around the mean. Most candidates understood what was required in the question, and were able to give the argument sketch required in part (b), but lost some marks for lacunae. Similarly, most received some but not all the marks available in part (c).

2018-6-6.examiner_comment: This question had a high number of attempts and a high median mark. Nearly all candidates got the 9 marks in part (b). Performance on part (d) was much more variable.

2018-6-7.examiner_comment: Generally good answers. Nearly everyone had a solid understanding of maximum likelihood estimation, and of resampling, which are the main points of the question. There were quite a few errors in (b) due to misplacing the 'n' term in the Central Limit Theorem. There were some sloppy answers to (d), which would be easily excusable if it weren't for the fact that a very similar problem was analysed in an example sheet.

2018-6-8.examiner_comment: Only two attempts. This is surprising - the question was mainly bookwork, so I assumed it would be seen as easy. Some guesses: * It's because mock exam questions were so late. [But then why did question 7 get more answers?] * Linear regression was taught in lectures 11-12. In Lecture 10 I gave them an outline of examinable material so far, which they may have interpreted as "linear regression is not examinable" * Maybe lectures 11 and 12 were too irregularly timetabled (a long gap after 10, and a gap between 11 and 12) for students to maintain attention. * Maybe students read through the entire question and saw that it combined two parts of the course in a way they hadn't expected, and were thrown.

2018-6-9.examiner_comment: Both exam questions went really well: I got loads of answer scripts, and this was the case for both questions. In case of question 9 on resolution, if I had to change something I would ask students to explicitly use linear binary resolution. Otherwise there is a good range of marks, and I have a feeling that the median is probably high, but the students studied and answered correctly. The questions were not too dissimilar to previous years, so it is a testament to the students that they studied for the course.

2018-7-2.examiner_comment: 26 scripts. Generally well answered, with most candidates getting marks in the first-class range. Some were clueless, however, whether about parts of the question or all of it; and some recited irrelevant bookwork. No update to solution notes.

2018-7-3.examiner_comment: There was no particular section of this question that the candidates struggled with or misunderstood. All candidates scored full marks for section (a). In section (b) many candidates were loose with terminology (referring to infinite sentences in many cases it was not clear that they knew that any given sentence has a finite length). Section (c) required a proof of 2 parts and many students did only one part of the proof (and this was not always the same part). Section (d) required "drawing the stack arising from a top-down parse"; several students did not draw a stack and many students attempted a bottom-up parse. Marks were awarded for any top-down parse rather than the exact model used by Yngve. In section (e) most candidates did not suggest sufficient justified alternatives to be awarded the full 4 marks.

2018-7-4.examiner_comment: Almost nobody got 4/4 on questions (a) or (b); I felt that this was fair, and separated top students from those below. But (a) could have been worded better to make it clear that both quality and speed should be justified. Questions (c)-(e) lacked nuance and should not have been weighted as heavily as they were.

2018-7-5.examiner_comment: This paper skewed high, and would have been better-weighted by making the coding problem worth 14 points and reducing all other question weights. Most students were able to answer (b) by rote. A surprising number of math errors cost points in (c).
topics: Surface Mesh Topology and Euler Characteristics

2018-7-6.examiner_comment: Most candidates noted main principles of goal directed search, and many gave detailed lists of heuristics and biases. Almost all identified the class of "wicked problems", nearly always illustrated with reference to climate change, although some attempted to discuss ludic design as "wicked", which is unconventional. No candidate really addressed the nature of Bayesian user models, mostly just discussing predictive text. Median 13, Mean 13.6, std dev 2.98

2018-7-7.examiner_comment: This was a straightforward design exercise, which candidates addressed very competently. Textual narrative explanations showed clear understanding of visual design basics. Median 16, mean 15.9, std dev 3.28

2018-7-8.examiner_comment: Median: 14. Most students made a reasonable attempt at the problem. Prolog provides an implementation of the modulus operator but some students implemented it themselves: full credit was given for both approaches. One common mistake was to forget that dividing by -1 results in a whole number result. Some attempts at part d were particularly verbose. This was due to the approach taken rather than a requirement of the question. Students with verbose but working answers were given full credit. Students who omitted parts of their solution (e.g. by saying similar for X) were only awarded partial credit.

2019-4-1.examiner_comment: Nearly all the students did well on the first half of this question, which could be solved by recalling basic facts about C programming: this part was probably a bit too easy. More students struggled with the second half of the question, which asked them to traverse and free a pointer graph. This is because success requires putting together several pieces -- traversing a graph, building a list of nodes, and then freeing a collection of composite objects. Overall the students demonstrated very good programming ability, and I think in future exams it is reasonable to cut back on the bookwork in favour of asking them to write programs of a similar level of complexity.
topics: Linked Lists and Data Structures in C

2019-4-2.examiner_comment: There were three parts to this question. The first was about undefined behaviour, the second about cache optimizations, and the third about C++. While most of the students identified some undefined behaviour, very few found it all, which suggests a bit more lecture time ought to be devoted to the topic. The cache optimization question was very all-or-nothing: those who got any marks got everything correct. I'm not sure what lesson to draw from this! The C++ question was another question where partial marks were the rule. This is less surprising, because C++ is so complicated that it's impossible to remember all the rules and their interactions.

2019-4-3.examiner_comment: Most students did well with (a)-(c). Many stumbled on (d) and (e). On (e) many sketched pictures of a stack, but no code. I will update my solution notes to discuss typical incorrect answers.

2019-4-4.examiner_comment: Conceptually more difficult than Question 3. Many students did not see how to typecheck the "raise" expression (b), and they had difficulty with the optimisation rules (c). I was fairly liberal in accepting reasonable solutions to (d). Again, I will update my solution notes to discuss typical errors.

2019-4-8.examiner_comment: This question tested whether they could execute and understand a semantics that they have not seen before, for a tiny C-like language. Part (a) asked them to evaluate the semantics on a concrete term - most did this pretty well, though only 16/84 did so perfectly. More supervision or example-class practice might be helpful. Part (b) was more variable. I didn't calculate the mean - it's probably high.

2019-4-9.examiner_comment: This question asked candidates to invent a reasonable subtype system for a tiny language with (vaguely) C-like integer types. As usual for the last question on the paper, a significant fraction clearly ran out of time, and this did demand a deeper understanding than Q8 - the mean will be lower.

2019-5-8.examiner_comment: The first 6 marks were a little too easy from bookwork, as many students surprisingly remembered all the conditions for deadlock and most explained it well. The last half of the question did pretty well to rank students; the format of a "bug finding" question worked well and there were fairly diverse answers. The median was pushed up by the easy first six marks, so in the future I'll increase the difficulty of bookwork questions.

2019-6-1.examiner_comment: Mostly candidates had a reasonable idea of how planning graphs work, however several shortcomings were common: In part (a) the representation given was often unnecessarily convoluted, and this tended to lead to problems later in the question. There was often confusion about the fact that the appropriate representation is propositional, and that introducing first-order elements, and specifically functions in the manner of a state-variable representation, was not appropriate. Some candidates avoided introducing negations, which made parts (c) and (d) somewhat tricky. In part (e) many candidates simply counted the number of actions needed for a solution to the problem but did not take account of their own representation. Many answers to part (f) essentially said "it makes the problem more complicated" - there was no credit for this, and such answers often failed to express "hard"-ness using an appropriate measure of complexity.

2019-6-2.examiner_comment: In part (a) many candidates lost out either by using the wrong planning language --- which carried over to the remainder of the question --- or by not giving examples as requested. In part (b) many simply defined heuristic search without addressing the question any further. In general marks were usually lost because this question involves taking one part of the course and applying it to material from another. Many candidates seemed to find this challenging.

2019-6-4.examiner_comment: The performance on this was disappointing. Even though a large number of students attempted it, the median mark was just 8. Many candidates did not get the idea for reduction from 3SAT to 4NAE required in part (c). But, what was more disappointing was the number of candidates that failed to get full marks in parts (a) and (b) which were bookwork questions, covering material explained in the lectures.

2019-6-5.examiner_comment: Statistics: 54 attempts, median mark = 11. This question examines material from the core of the course. Part (a) asks for a standard definition; a common error was to define a universal machine for k-ary functions for a fixed k, rather than (as asked), one that is universal for functions of any arity. Part (d) asks the candidate for a proof of a result not covered in the course (Kleene's second recursion theorem), but provides a detailed hint. A good number of candidates were successful in part (d). A common error among those who were not was to jump to the conclusion that the equality of the partial functions with indexes e and e' implies that e and e' are equal numbers.

2019-6-6.examiner_comment: Statistics: 54 attempts, median mark = 11. This question examines material from the core of the course. Part (a) asks for a standard definition; a common error was to define a universal machine for k-ary functions for a fixed k, rather than (as asked), one that is universal for functions of any arity. Part (d) asks the candidate for a proof of a result not covered in the course (Kleene's second recursion theorem), but provides a detailed hint. A good number of candidates were successful in part (d). A common error among those who were not was to jump to the conclusion that the equality of the partial functions with indexes e and e' implies that e and e' are equal numbers.

2019-6-7.examiner_comment: Students did fine on (a) and (b), started well on (c) but struggled to complete it, really struggled with (d) with the top mark being 3/5, and made good attempts at (e). It seems that nearly all students understood the concepts (Bayes's rule to find the posterior, then marginalize out unknown variables), but they struggled to materialize the concept in an equation to be solved. In retrospect, (d) was too hard -- if they made any mistakes in (c), they were disadvantaged for (d).

2019-6-8.examiner_comment: This question had generally good answers. There was a clear progression in difficulty in the parts, from (a) which everyone got right, to (e) which only two got right. Nearly all the answers showed some reasonable understanding of the concepts involved (linear models, orthogonality, resampling). The main difficulties were in (c) where it takes careful thought to combine the code's outputs in the right way, though some students just got lucky given how they chose to answer (b); and in (e) where I think most students lost their nerve and couldn't reconcile the general definition of "confidence interval" with an unfamiliar setting.

2019-6-9.examiner_comment: This question was attempted by practically all candidates (94). For those who knew what they were doing, a perfect score could be obtained without excessive writing or calculations. However, a good many students attempted this question without being properly prepared for it.

2019-6-10.examiner_comment: This question was attempted by practically all candidates (94). For those who knew what they were doing, a perfect score could be obtained without excessive writing or calculations. However, a good many students attempted this question without being properly prepared for it.

2019-7-2.examiner_comment: Mean=13.1, Median=14, SD=3.7, Range=3-20. a) This question was bookwork and most scored highly. b) The really good answers explained why second price auctions incentivised honest bidding. Most identified ad quality and click rates as being important. A minority talked about other parts of the course, e.g. consumer surplus. Fewer still gave answers that had not been covered/were irrelevant. c) Most gave reasonable answers to this question, but there was some variance in how well they argued their points. Some referred to recent political events (e.g. US elections/EU referendum) as examples, which were not relevant for marking purposes. d) Most were able to correctly describe bidding rings. The really good answers were those that identified the need for repeated games using the tit-for-tat strategy.

2019-7-3.examiner_comment: Mean=12.5, Median=12, SD=3.6, Range=5-19. a) This section was bookwork, and was mostly correct. b) This section applied a) to a specific scenario. There were some really good answers, but most missed one or more relevant aspects. c) This question was hit or miss. Some students did not attempt it at all, or gave irrelevant answers. Others were aptly able to demonstrate their understanding of the case, and a few were able to explain how it was relevant to b).
topics: Legal Frameworks for Data and Technology

2019-7-4.examiner_comment: The majority of students provided an answer to all parts of this question. Most students scored well in the first sections, applying the entropy equation—students were only penalised once for using the wrong base (and the majority got this correct). The question regarding the entropy of the language was bookwork but credit was given where a student had tried to derive something using entropy rate. Descriptions of the noisy channel ranged from very poor to excellent. Good answers closely adhered to the question (referring to human communication). For the last sections of the question good answers tended to be those that made correct reference to aspects of information theory.

2019-7-5.examiner_comment: Despite being lectured only on Lexical Tree Adjoining Grammars (TAGs) a reasonable number of students produced non-Lexical TAGs instead. Also a surprisingly high number of students defined a Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) that was only weakly equivalent to their TAG. This meant that their CCG had unusual and non-sensical categories (e.g. one noun was typed as an N but the other noun was given a complex category). In both cases marks were awarded for any working grammar that could parse the sentence. But candidates who adopted these approaches tended to lose marks in the other parts of the question where their discussion became muddled/inconsistent with their linguistic knowledge.
topics: Syntax Trees and Tree Adjoining Grammars

2019-7-6.examiner_comment: p7q6 gave students who were strong in VR, or in geometry, or in glsl, a chance to shine; few were strong in all topics. I felt this was a tough but effective question.
topics: Surface Mesh Topology and Euler Characteristics

2019-7-7.examiner_comment: p7q7 was too binary--students either did quite well or quite poorly with few in the middle ground. I felt this question was a little too easy.

2019-7-8.examiner_comment: This is the first time that we have experimented with asking students to reflect on their own practical coursework in an examination question. It seems to have worked OK, but a small number of students focused only on describing what they did do, rather than responding to questions about what they *could* have done, or *would* do in future. This had the effect that some did not refer to appropriate areas of the curriculum, focusing instead on things that they had done but were not in the curriculum. If similar questions are used in future, the introduction to the question should make clear that students are being asked to think about how things might be done differently, based on what they have learned in the course.

2019-7-9.examiner_comment: This was a challenging question that was answered very well on the whole, showing that it relates to specific interests of Cambridge students, and perhaps also to the research interests of supervisors who contributed most to this course. The "three waves" in the history of HCI seems to resonate with students, and relating them to the changing perspectives on usability of programming languages has been effective.

topics: Linked Lists and Data Structures in C
Surface Mesh Topology and Euler Characteristics

2021-4-1.examiner_comment: A worryingly large number of candidates forgot that the stack is dynamic and considered local vars to main() to be static. Some material returned by Google is wrong in this respect. Many answers for the base32 encoding used two characters for every byte. Although an efficiency requirement was not specified in the question, this was awarded 4 out 5.
topics: Dynamic Memory Allocation and Custom Management

2021-4-2.examiner_comment: Part (a) The very best answers checked whether a new value could be stored over an old value because bits were only being set (e.g. a longer string in a fixed-length pre-allocated slot). Several of the poorer answers just stored string pointers in the NV store instead of the strings themselves or relied on a volatile pointer to the next free space in NV store. Part (b)(i) well-answered question on difference between C++ and Java meaning of "Foo x;". Part(b)(ii) explored debugging via constructors, destructors and overloading assignment -- gave a good range of marks.

2021-4-3.examiner_comment: There are 15 marks for a programming exercise for which many students provided only a minimal answer. To me, this shows that students have not been extending the toy compiler. If they had been doing practical work on the toy compiler this question would have been easy. In fact, I thought that this question was the easier of q3 and q4.

2021-4-8.examiner_comment: I was pleasantly surprised that, students did much better on this question than I expected. Nearly everyone did well on formulating the operational semantics, and most did nearly as well with the type system for the language. The place where students struggled was in adapting the definition of type safety to the new language.

2021-4-9.examiner_comment: Overall, students did extremely well on this question, considerably surpassing my expectations. The main thing they struggled with was part Ii of a), which called for a proof. Many students tried to supply a proof which followed the exact structure of the definition of semantic equivalence rather than observing that the two programs would become equal in three steps.

2021-5-4.examiner_comment: Small variations in answers to a,b,c minimally penalised, most errors in part c due to consistent misreading of the question (mistaking switch for router, or misunderstanding that layer-2 switches are full participants throughout the entire network.) Due to a lack of specific constraint a number of (less relevant) answers to part d were given, these were marked correct as appropriate and these additional information/alternatives will be given in model answers. In the future, lengthy scoping would remove such out-of-scope answers.

2021-5-5.examiner_comment: A transcription error led in c(i) to an unexpected, non-trivial, answer. All answers to this part were considered liberally as a result. Actual effect was practically in the range of 0-2 marks.

2021-5-6.examiner_comment: A question not answered by a significant portion of the cohort - possibly because IPv6 still remains (After 5 years) a new subtopic. A disappointing set of results with a question intended to cause a fused answer covering IPv6 addresses, network routing in IP (first part) and then line coding in the second part. Some very disappointing answers relating to the confusion of the link-layer (physical) but also some excellent and thoughtful answers too.

2021-5-7.examiner_comment: Candidates found this question quite easy, especially the definition of strict vs non-strict isolation.

2021-5-8.examiner_comment: I revamped the distributed systems course in Michaelmas 2020, and this exam question drew from the new syllabus. I was a bit disappointed with this set of answers, especially on part (d). Many students did not really critically engage with the problem and appeared not to fully appreciate the impact of unbounded network delay and execution pauses on distributed algorithms, even though this is a point I repeatedly emphasised in lectures. I will try adding supervision exercises around this point next year, to get students thinking about it. Due to the open-book nature of the exam I designed the question so that not many marks could be gained by mere bookwork; I think this resulted in lower marks for the weaker students who didn't have easy bookwork marks to raise their score. Overall, I think the question successfully tested the students' skill at reasoning about the behaviour of distributed systems.

2021-6-1.examiner_comment: A somewhat disappointing median mark, given that 9 marks could be gained for parts (a) and (c) alone, which were essentially undemanding. Observations: In (a) many provided derivatives but no algorithm, and many forgot to include $b$ in the calculation. Unfortunately many cases showed an Inability to differentiate. Answers to (b) often had a workable starting point, but for example used ||w||-1 without squaring. Again in several cases there was an inability to differentiate. Several answers did not introduce a hyperparameter. In (c) many answered a question that wasn't asked, for example, talking about A^* specifically, or admissibility and so on, or talking about heuristics, not heuristic search problems. In (d) many had a basically useable starting point but insufficient detail, made only one suggestion, and/or did not addresses possible disadvantages.

2021-6-2.examiner_comment: Generally quite well answered. In part (b) many ignored the instruction that there should be $n$ variables and so on. In (c) many didn't realise that two constraints are already binary, and some did not provide a graph. In (e) some missed out the auxiliary variable or applied constraint propagation prematurely, modifying the domain of x_4 when assigning x_2, when they are not in a constraint.

2021-6-3.examiner_comment: The level of difficulty of this question was about right. Part (a) was quite elementary, and most students got full marks with some exceptions. Only one student who provided an answer to this part did not get any partial marks and received a 0. Part (b) was the most challenging, however most students were able to receive at least 6/12 marks by correctly proving one direction of implication. Very few students received full marks for this part, but all who wrote something for it received at least some partial marks. Part (c) saw the most varied responses of all, and likewise the marks were the most varied. Overall the students fared well however and most received full marks for this part.

2021-6-4.examiner_comment: The level of difficulty of this question was about right. Part (a) was straightforward and most students were awarded full marks. Marks were lost here when students did not clearly state whether the statement is true, false, or unknown; when they did so incorrectly; or when their justification was insufficient. Part (b) had quite varied results, mostly because roughly half of the students proved the wrong direction of implication. Part (c)(i) was again straightforward and students received full marks as long as they correctly and clearly described that the certificate is an assignment to the unknowns and the verification is done via a computation of each of the equations. Part (c)(ii) was the most challenging for students. About half of the students did not even attempt the question, and of those who did, only one student received full marks. Note the median was 0.

2021-6-5.examiner_comment: A question where reading and understanding the notation is half the battle. Candidates who did not time out gave reasonably good answers to both (a) and (b) with the hint at the start of (b)(ii) rendering it do-able. A common error in part (a) was to forget to explain why the S-m-n function is total.

2021-6-6.examiner_comment: Traditionally students find questions on the last third of the course material (such as this one), quite challenging; on top of which the question is about a topic, combinatory algebras, not covered in lectures. Nevertheless, the question was quite well answered by a reasonable number of candidates. However, all but one missed the fact that in part (a) the question asks about beta-equivalence classes of lambda terms and so lost marks for not noting the fact that application is a congruence for beta-equivalence.

2021-6-7.examiner_comment: I adjusted the mark scheme. Nearly all the attempts did a(i) and a(ii) in the brute force way, not the shortcut I was expecting, so it took them longer than I anticipated. Without this adjustment, students at the low end would have scored very poorly.

2021-6-8.examiner_comment: All parts of this question had some good and some bad answers. For part (a.ii) roughly half the students failed to properly distinguish between a confidence interval and a test. In retrospect I think (b) should have included a bit more ML rather than pure probability.

2021-6-9.examiner_comment: Produced a broad range of marks. The final part was slightly easier than anticipated, resulting in a relatively high median mark.

2021-6-10.examiner_comment: Probably too easy, as evidenced by the numerous perfect scores. But attempted by fewer candidates than the other Logic and Proof question.

2021-7-2.examiner_comment: The median mark is 12, mainly because many students did poorly with respect to question a) ii). Many students obviously copy and pasted what information they had about GDPR (it looked like from last year's exam question) without carefully reading the question. Therefore, many students missed that GDPR provides individuals with rights about automate decision making. The students who identified this tended to do quite well at this question.

topics: Legal Frameworks for Data and Technology

2021-7-4.examiner_comment: (a) (i) Around half of the students interpreted the question as requiring a known fixed n as opposed to n \in N. Both were marked as corrected but then consistency with their choice was required throughout this part of the question. (ii) Generally answered well. Some defined the grammar explicitly while others through a mapping with the DFA in (i). Common errors included: forgetting to handle the end state; including rules to a null state; not using regular grammar rules. (iii) Any reasonable answer was given a mark. Quite a large number of students didn't attempt an answer to this part. (b) (i) Quite a few students didn't read the question and failed to extend the example given. (ii) Generally answered badly. Was marked generously such that all relevant statements were given a mark, up to 3 marks. There was a lot of confusion over the various types of grammars and what the pumping lemme can and cannot prove. (iv) On the whole answered well. Common errors included: forgetting to terminate the grammar; and non-confirmation to CNF. (v) Also answered reasonably well. Most students realised how to use the stack to achieve equal numbers of Nouns and Verbs. Several students answered generally rather than with relevance to the question—they only lost one mark for this. A common mistake was to accept a string of verbs without any nouns.

2021-7-5.examiner_comment: (a) Most students gained full marked. Some didn't draw the full tree and a small number could only find one tree. (b) Majority of students knew how to find the probability of a single derivation but a large number did not remember that they needed to sum over all derivations in order to find the probability of a string. (c) Most answered fully. Some students only found one derivation of length 4 and a very small number found spurious derivations. (d) Most answered quite well. A large number of times the DFA was correct but the regular expression was wrong or didn't match. A common error for the DFA was to miss the string 'av' (I had missed it myself in the model answer!) or not to ensure a 'h' was always followed by a 'v'. (e) Not answered well, generally. Most students had some gap in their reasoning or a non-trivial mistake. Several assumed independence and non-independence of the same variables at different points in their answer. Some looked at conditional entropy of the L_i language sequence—although the question didn't ask for this, since the reasoning was similar, they were given marks for displaying the right knowledge. (f) Generally answered poorly and I marked this generously. There was rarely a clear hypothesis or reason. In the end 1 mark was awarded for describing something relevant and another clearly linking to the question or explaining how the hypothesis might be tested. There were one or two very good answers.

2021-7-6.examiner_comment: Except the three students who tried to answer only the questions a and b and did not continue, all students got marks above or equal to the median.
topics: Surface Mesh Topology and Euler Characteristics

2021-7-7.examiner_comment: This question was attempted by not many students. Some of the students who got low marks probably did not consider all sub-questions before starting to answer and thus could answer the first easier question correctly, but not the others.

2021-7-8.examiner_comment: All parts were answered well, with open book access meaning that most candidates were able to apply terminology from the course. Part a) was similar to an example from lectures, with most candidates able to answer correctly, so one mark was reserved for original insights. In part c) many candidates explained variability due to individual differences in preference or skill, rather than addressing experimental validity or the logic of null hypothesis testing. In part d) goal-directed search could be used to describe how the feature is turned on, but isn't sufficient as a model of programming. Some answers, apparently distracted by the word "cognitive", only summarised cognitive walkthrough or cognitive dimensions.

2021-7-9.examiner_comment: Most candidates did well overall. Although part a) was intended as an easy mark, some candidates did not address functional registration to physical objects, or confused AR and VR (perhaps had not heard of Hololens - though could easily have looked it up). I had to mark part b) flexibly, where students had misunderstood part a). In part c), identifying relevant resources was relatively trivial, and got easy marks. Part d) was a bit too easy given access to online lists of dimensions, and clear difference between visual and speech interfaces. While in other years, I might give partial marks for naming a dimension without good explanation of its relevance, I did not do so this year in order to avoid "bookwork" answers. Part e) was a challenging research question - most candidates got part marks for describing design field research methods, but a few produced interesting ideas.

2021-7-10.examiner_comment: As a general trend the code written by candidates had fewer mistakes than previous years - perhaps due to candidates having access to a Prolog interpreter whilst taking the exam. A noticeable proportion of candidates lost marks by failing to provide declarative comments for their predicates as required by the question. Another common mistake was neglecting that 'charAt' required the index parameter to be ground. On the flip side a good number of students successfully navigated this very well with an iterative deepening strategy in the final part of the question. In about 1/3rd of scripts candidates misinterpreted the final part of the question to be about recovering a key given two single characters (one plaintext, one ciphertext). The wording of the question did not prohibit this and so even though I consider it as an unlikely interpretation given the scenario of the question full credit was given. Candidates came up with a variety of strategies for dealing with the circular alphabet in part b - all working approaches were given credit.

2022-4-1.examiner_comment: (a) and (b) should be easy. (c) full marks for initial rewrite. 2 lost marks of continued rewrite on prefixes that match from right-hand-side of different non-terminals. (d) full marks for a rewrite rule, 2 lost marks for doing this on different non-terminals sharing a prefix. (e) 2 marks for if, 2 marks for only if. The problem asks students to "argue carefully" so hand waving ("it works because it obviously works") gets 0 marks.

2022-4-2.examiner_comment: Parts (a), (b), and (c) are direct applications of lecture material and so most students did well. Part (d) tested the students understanding of CPS, and very few identified the issue. Many confused defunctionalizing the continuation with defunctionalizing the argument f (which we really don't want or need to do).

2022-4-4.examiner_comment: In part (a), many candidates repeated the distinctions outlined in the question, but no credit was awarded for that. In part (b), virtually nobody separated out the key and value aspects, but clearly having the key change under the feet of the key/value store might upset its indexing structure whereas this could be considered useful for the value. In part (c), a number of candidates noted that a string pointer initialised with a literal string typically has immutable content, whereas a normal C array is mutable. There was not really relevant. In part (d), a lot of candidates failed to adequately distinguish between compile-time and run-time behaviour.

2022-4-5.examiner_comment: In part (a), some candidates did not appreciate that items are removed from the head of a queue and new arrivals join the tail: there was a lot of adding to the head. Some implemented a doubly-linked list, but it should be clear this is not needed for a FIFO. Moreover, for the free list in part (b), nearly all candidates felt that this required head and tail pointers and strangely believed it should maintain FIFO order. Some candidates chained along their lists for every operation. Some candidates used malloc and free in their implementation of the free list, defeating its whole purpose. I will point out these disappointing and fundamental failures in next year's lecture materials. Part (c) showed most students could use new/delete for C++, but many did not take on board the full implications of "not possible to create an instance" (i.e. having private/deleted constructor and only static members). Part (d) was disappointingly answered given the Java generic erasure model (taught in Part 1A) contrasts with macro-style C++ templates and students had access to Java and C++ compilers for testing.
topics: Linked Lists and Data Structures in C

2022-4-8.examiner_comment: Most students did very well with the proof of reflexivity, whereas the difficulty of the proof of transitivity of subtyping was considerably harder. The main difficulty was correctly identifying what to induction over, and then correctly formulating a viable induction hypothesis.

2022-4-9.examiner_comment: Overall, most students were able to identify the error in the language design, and with a bit more struggle were able to figure out one of many reasonable fixes to the problem. By and large, the students struggled with finding the correct formulation of type safety for this language: they often forgot to check that the runtime bindings matched the compile-time type declarations, which would have made it impossible to prove type safety.

2022-5-1.examiner_comment: A challenging question with a wide variety of interpretations. For example there are two distinct approaches to the algorithm of (b). Some students did not seem to remember basic geometry (circumference etc.) which was surprising. Additional assessment guidance will be added to marking guide for this question.

2022-5-2.examiner_comment: Considerable evidence candidates left this question until "last" - a significant number of students where no attempts were made on section c - leading to very skewed outcomes (c is worth half the marks for this question). Candidate 2208D answers were misfiled and his Q3 answers are in the Q3 spread sheet.

2022-5-4.examiner_comment: In part (a), some students equated lock ordering for deadlock avoidance with thread priority ordering. But these are largely independent when threads and lock interactions are relatively sparse or unpredictable. In part (c) Only 26/99 of attempts had clearly understood 'message passing' to denote reliable message passing under the actor model. 39/96 seemed to have forgotten that topic was on the syllabus and instead interpreted part (c) of the question to be about consensus in distributed systems. Full credit could be achieved either way.

2022-5-5.examiner_comment: Both parts of the question asked students to design their own protocol meeting specified criteria, using building blocks explained during the course. Students engaged well with this question, resulting in a good distribution of marks.

2022-5-6.examiner_comment: Many students produced a solid but slightly less optimal solution, but obtained high marks. Weaker answers made some surprising use of ripple counters and clock gating.

2022-5-7.examiner_comment: Candidates generally did well on this question, so the median is a little high. Part (b) turned out to be slight ambiguous, so it could be correctly answered two different ways. One approach (the one the original model answer follows) is to assume that byte addresses are used (which is common), but this does result in unaligned memory accesses (which is less common on RISC processors). To avoid unaligned accesses, some people chose word addressing. It was always clear what choice people had made so the ambiguity caused no difficulty.

2022-5-8.examiner_comment: (b) While memory "speed" was mentioned, few mentioned DRAM bandwidth in their answer so I had to adjust my marking scheme. (d) Several candidates explained how conditional program flow works on GPUs but failed to provide an explanation for CPUs, which was surprising.

2022-6-1.examiner_comment: Generally answered well, and this is reflected in the high median. Many confused "heuristic" with "heuristic search".

2022-6-2.examiner_comment: Generally done very well indeed, as suggested by the high median.

2022-6-3.examiner_comment: There was a wide spread of marks, with a median of 12, which suggests that the question struck the right level of difficulty. Some of the questions (parts (a) and (b) in particcular), could be answered by looking up appropriate notes or online resources. But, this does not seem to have helped candidates who lacked an understanding of what to look for. Indeed, some candidates did reproduce bits of the notes or textbook sources but taken out of context, they did not make much sense as answers and did not receive much credit.

2022-6-4.examiner_comment: The question invited the candidates to explore the complexity of the Graph Homomorphism problem. This problem had not been explicitly discussed in the lectures. The vast majority of candidates were able to recognise that the problem is NP-complete. This was established in Parts (a), (b) and (c) of the question. Similarly, most candidates realised that the special case identified in Part (d) is in P. Many candidates who did recognise why the arguments they were asked to construct in Parts (a), (b) and (c) implied NP-completeness still failed to articulate a clear mathematical argument and so lost some marks as a result. For instance, quite a few candidates stated in Part (c) that a reduction from 3-colourability to HOM was established without stating what the reduction was. A small number of candidates got perfect marks.

2022-6-5.examiner_comment: I have no explanation for why there is such a low median mark for this question. It asks the candidate to prove or disprove some standard facts of computation theory about the concept of "recursively enumerable" sets of numbers. Although the topic is not covered in lectures explicitly, it features in several past questions. The Examiners asked me to change the initial version of the question by removing mention of the term "recursively enumerable", in order to prevent candidates just searching on-line for the standard facts about which the question asks. The result is a question that is still not very hard, based on my past experience. And yet here we have a set of attempts that contain far too many that are appallingly bad. Even discounting the scripts which did not attempt to answer all parts, too many answers displayed a very poor grasp of what is or is not computable in principle (and a few displayed a poor grasp of logic, claiming that part (d) (of the form "does A imply B?") is the same as part (b) (of the form "does B imply A?"). At least there were 7 candidates who gave very good answers.

2022-6-6.examiner_comment: This is a question about the last third of the course, lambda calculus. It leads the candidate step by step to a classic result not covered in the course (undecidability of existence of a beta-normal form). The question is designed so that each step is not very hard, but there is quite a bit of unfamiliar notation to take in along the way. Many candidates answered quite well and the scripts with low marks are mostly from candidates who did not attempt most of the question.

2022-6-7.examiner_comment: A decent spread of answers. For each of the three parts, students either knew the material and had little trouble, or didn't know the material and had no idea where to start. (And a couple of students had such poor maths ability that they wasted too much effort on algebra.)

2022-6-8.examiner_comment: In retrospect, this question was too hard. The first two parts were fine, but (c) needed good fluency in algebra, and (d) depended too much on (c). I would like to suggest reweighting the marks, as per column M (10 marks for a and b, 10 marks for c and d), if the examiners find this acceptable.

2022-6-9.examiner_comment: Somewhat to my surprise, the expected median was hit dead on. Nevertheless, the best students could score a 20. No book work was requested or wanted, but unfortunately a fair bit was offered.

2022-6-10.examiner_comment: This question clearly had some easy parts and some difficult parts while hitting the desired medium fairly closely.

2022-7-2.examiner_comment: In relation to Part A, I awarded marks to the students who noted that it is more difficult to gain entry to the market for handset providers, which is essentially a oligopoly. Some students misread handset as headset, but the general principles remain the same, except for 2b, where these are not necessarily complementary assets, but students did not lose marks for this.

2022-7-3.examiner_comment: Students struggled with part a) the most, however those that recognised the importance of behavioural economics in framing did quite well. I awarded points for other convincing arguments. Students did much better in part b), although points for not awarded for suggestions that the webmail provider should unquestionably hand over the emails to the police if asked, or the police should hack into the accounts.
topics: Legal Frameworks for Data and Technology

2022-7-4.examiner_comment: a) answered well by most b) many students forgot the repeat state c) most common mistake was to not consider the compatible sentences. The answer was fiddly so mistakes were tolerated where there was evidence of considering the input d) most common mistake was to omit the first step e) mostly answered well f) some students provided an algorithm that changed the paradigm. Most did not provide many points of regarding the assumptions of the learning paradigm with respect to human language learning.

2022-7-5.examiner_comment: On the whole I was impressed with how the students attempted this question. For the most part they successfully gained 2 marks for (a)(i). For (a)(ii) they also usually gained all available marks: a common shortcoming here was in failing to mention the kind of training data required. For (a)(iii) most students identified the problem of out-of-vocabulary words and presented solutions which showed good lateral thinking (as well as knowledge gained during lectures). In (b) the majority of students successfully described a noisy channel approach to error correction: the usual shortcomings being a failure to mention training data or _correction_ (rather than just detection of errors). The students did quite well with (c) but sometimes did not correctly apply the error modelling part of the equation. The students did very well with (d) but sometimes failed to make 4 distinct points about similarities and differences, or didn't fully describe or justify the point they were trying to make.

2022-7-6.examiner_comment: There are 7 students with marks <= 15, so the median is almost 15. Originally, we had one more subquestion in this question, which I removed after discussions, which might have led to an increase in the median.

2022-7-8.examiner_comment: Candidates engaged enthusiastically with this question, and none failed to understand the basic premise. The median mark was high as a result, and I was impressed overall. In part c, I therefore penalised minor errors of interpretation that would probably have got full marks in previous years. Quite a few presented the three analogical features in part a, but forgot to explain the design idea, for which 2 marks were lost.

2022-7-9.examiner_comment: Part a: diverse answers, many not spotting the value of open and qualitative methods in formative research. A surprising number suggest that cognitive walkthrough can be used to analyse qualitative data, and that task flow diagrams are the best way to present it, neither of which is recommended in this course. The focus on weather apps in some answers suggests confusion with Part 1a Interaction Design. Part b: surprisingly few suggested the machine learning approach of inferring repeated actions. Marks were given for any design ideas, although very few included interesting theoretical analysis. Many failed to notice the key words "attention and decisions" as the focus of analysis. Part c: answered OK, and marked leniently. Part d: many failed to understand implications of a focus on efficiency.

2023-4-1.examiner_comment: This very popular question (102 submissions) was answered well overall. Students were generally able to determine whether grammars described LL(1) languages, but identifying grammatical ambiguity question proved more challenging, with only around a fifth of students answering entirely correctly. On part (d), lots of answers correctly identified the circumstances where the proposed simplifications were correct for optimisation, but many had difficulties with correctness for type checking, with only a handful achieving full marks.

2023-4-2.examiner_comment: This was slightly less popular than q1, with 80 submissions. The first three parts were mechanical applications of transformations covered in the course (CPS conversion, defunctionalization, defunctionalization adjusted to use lists), and students performed well, with almost half scoring full marks on both of the first two parts. A surprising number of students struggled with transforming defunctionalized code to use lists, which was in principle the simplest part of the question.

2023-4-4.examiner_comment: In setting the question I might have underestimated the change from internet exams to internal and the students found the Prolog question harder this year than last. Even so a handful of students aced the question but there is quite a spread. There are a couple of students with very low marks but they seem to have shot in a quick answer mainly for parts (a) and (b) presumably to grab a couple of extra points for the paper as a whole, and this reduces the median a little.

topics: Dynamic Memory Allocation and Custom Management

2023-4-7.examiner_comment: This question, on attack surfaces and privilege escalation, attracted about 50 scripts. On the whole the quality of the answers was disappointing, with too many students parroting memorable sound bites but without demonstrating true understanding or ability to apply the concepts to concrete cases. The resulting median of 9/20 was thus below the desired range. Although syntactic mistakes in Python and LaTeX were not penalised, several candidates denoted a frightening lack of familiarity with either language, quite surprising for second-year computer science students. Part (a) was the most difficult and worst-answered of the lot, with only a couple of students able to make good use of the UTF-8 hint. Partial credit was given to those who offered a thorough analysis to back up their answer, even if wrong. Parts (b) and (d) had some proportion of decent answers. Strangely, despite the limitless variety of LaTeX syntax errors that would have earned a very easy 3 marks in part (b) (such as inserting a random invalid command, as some did), a few too many students, for reasons unknown, chose a very specific example that does NOT in itself raise an error but simply causes the rest of the input to be ignored. Full credit was still given to those who observed that an error would eventually be raised IF truncating the file in this way caused mismatched begin-end pairs (or braces) of any kind. Part (c), where the question tolerated ad-hoc fixes that would not have worked in the general case, was perhaps the easiest, and generally well answered. Part (e), more essay-style and with many marks awarded, was generally OK and allowed some weaker candidates to rescue their poor answers from parts (a)-(d), although few candidates achieved full marks for this part.

2023-4-8.examiner_comment: This question, on master keying, attracted about 50 scripts. On the whole, students demonstrated a reasonable grasp of the relevant concepts. The median of the marks (12/20) was within the expected range. Part (a) was fairly open and there were many opportunities for earning the available marks in many different ways, which students took advantage of. The weaker candidates were unable to provide actual scenarios for the end of that sub question, sticking to generic platitudes rather than mentioning concrete use cases; but, overall, many students got high marks here. Part (b.i) was the easiest and most students got full marks. For part (b.ii), most students were able to list the 8 keys that would definitely open the lock but very few noted that there could in theory be others. Part (b.iii) required a good understanding of the Blaze attack and did a good job of separating those who fully understood it from those who attempted to handwave their way through it.

2023-5-1.examiner_comment: Many decent attempts with good range. However, a notable number of students that failed to read the question and - as a result - only provided partial answers.

2023-5-2.examiner_comment: Regrettable omission in part of the question (failing to specify a work-stealing/work-conserving approach) has removed much fidelity in the mark-range. Additionally, this also accounts for a higher than desirable median mark. Mea Culpa.

2023-5-3.examiner_comment: Possibly a little easier than intended with some bunching in the higher distribution of marks.

2023-5-5.examiner_comment: Several strong answers, but median result is low. Submissions suggested candidates generally understood the problem well and mapped it to distributed algorithms from the course. However, answers for b(i)-b(ii) were often correct in the error-free cases, but did not handle the requirement of "fair loss" links -- for instance, the need to reject messages that were duplicated in the network, or to handle message loss, or to be robust to messages delivered long after transmission. With hindsight, standard definitions in a(i)--(iii) probably too detailed for 1 mark each -- many "1/2-mark" responses covering one main point but missing another.

2023-5-6.examiner_comment: Students performed quite well on this question though a few had such a poor understanding of the SystemVerilog code at the start of the question that they obtained very few marks. I was surprised that students attempted the question if they did not have a firm grasp of SystemVerilog. There is a small error in the question that was identified in the exam: the signature for module seqB names the output "a" when it should have been "b". I saw no evidence in answers that this caused confusion.

2023-5-7.examiner_comment: This was a popular question despite it not being easy. Many students made minor errors (which were ignored) when writing RISC-V assembler. In particular, forgetting that the first argument of an R-type instruction is always the destination register not the first operand, and incorrect syntax for addressing despite the example in Part (b). In part (b), many students identified that load hoisting was a good idea, but very few noticed that load/store words could be replaced by load/store double in order halve the size of the code. In part (c), many students said that an additional temporary register would be required to implement the swap instruction in hardware despite them identifying a sequence of instructions that perform swap without using a temporary register in part (d).

2023-5-8.examiner_comment: Very few students answered all parts of this question thoroughly. In particular, voltage/frequency scaling was poorly understood. Answers to part (d) were also poor. Many answers were poorly constructed, demonstrating poor exam. technique. The marking scheme was adjusted accordingly.

2023-6-3.examiner_comment: Parts (a)-(c) are easy standard material and there is little excuse for not getting the full 9 marks; nevertheless, a large number of candidates did badly on these parts, giving imprecise or incorrect definitions. Part (d) introduces a concept not covered in the course and (d)(ii) in particular is quite challenging to do under exam conditions (so I marked generously); nevertheless, several candidates answered it very well.

2023-6-4.examiner_comment: This question examines the last third of the course, which is on lambda calculus and is traditionally less popular than the rest of the course (witness the smaller number of attempts compared with q3). However, for those who like this material, the questions asked here are not too difficult, being some standard results plus some simple variations on material covered in lectures. Few candidates gave a completely correct answer for part (b), almost all forgetting to say that the representing lambda term has to be closed.

2023-6-5.examiner_comment: Parts (a) and (b) were well answered. Nearly all students wrote down appropriate models; roughly half of them did it the elegant way (linear regression) and half did it hackily (explicit likelihood maximization or loss minimization, splitting the data in half for the piecewise fit). At least they all understood the big picture, even if they didn't all have deftness. Part (c) had poor answers on the whole -- but it was asking them to do something I don't explicitly teach, so I'm glad that about half of them basically got the point that some sort of resampling approach is appropriate.

2023-6-6.examiner_comment: The question worked well. It had lots of pieces, and different students got right a different mix of pieces. I was very pleased to see that a large number of students were creative enough to invent a useful test statistic for (b). The only particularly tricky part was in part (c) where only one student spotted that the initial (equilibrium) value was informative about the probability model.

2023-6-7.examiner_comment: Generally, part (a) was as expected, most students did very well. In general Part (b) was more difficult, and in particular Part (b)(i) caused more problems as the students had to figure out whether something was satisfiable and provide a model, or whether it was unsatisfiable and provide a proof, so getting it wrong meant that they would try to construct models that could just not possibly work. The students that got it right usually found that there were three formulas that were contradictory, and finding a proof using only those three formulas was much easier than trying to work with all of the formulas without knowing which were relevant. A sizeable group did not even attempt to answer this part. For part (b)(ii) most got it right. Those that did not modelled the formulae incorrectly without trying to find the satisfiability of the negation of the formulae. Generally, part (b)(i) was the trickiest for the students, but also for marking.

2023-6-8.examiner_comment: Everything was as expected. Common mistakes were forgetting to negate the formula at the start (proof by contradiction), didn't solemnise correctly, or forgot to give a counterexample.

2023-6-9.examiner_comment: Overall, students did reasonably well on this question. The main things that they struggled with was the realisation that since the language had no store or variables, it was possible to remove the context from the typing judgement and the store from the operational semantics. Those that had this insight generally did extremely well, making errors only minor details like checking whether the fields of the product of two relations were disjoint.

2023-6-10.examiner_comment: The distribution of marks in this problem was strongly bimodal -- students typically did very well, or very poorly. The major hurdle was realizing that part (a) was actually a question asking how to model the printing effect, and students who realised that they were free to invent a semantics typically did quite well on the remainder. This also required students to adjust the formulation of the progress theorem, though the proof itself was largely unchanged from lecture.

2023-7-1.examiner_comment: The question involved discussing a simple problem designed to be very directly translatable to state variable representation. While the initial parts were usually well-done many candidates conflated this particular representation with other planning methods such as situation calculus. Many similarly suffered because they failed to use the core part of the method, which involves functions as opposed to predicates. The translation to a CSP was often done quite well when the basics had been properly appreciated but fell apart quickly otherwise. Hence the wide spread of marks (0 to 20) but the somewhat disappointing median of 9.

2023-7-2.examiner_comment: Parts (a) and (b) were mostly done quite well. However many candidates attempted part (c) by trying to apply the chain rule without realising that they needed to use the general variant summing over several terms. (This isn't necessary if you take the approach used in the solution notes, but many tried a different route.)

2023-7-3.examiner_comment: There was some confusion in interpreting part a), in that many responses answered about philosophies of ethics, rather than the 6 branches of philosophy. I can see why this confusion may have occurred in an exam situation, and it is possible to obtain full marks if different 'flavours' of ethical philosophies are counted. I therefore marked those that had mis-interpreted the question as if the question was as they had assumed.

2023-7-4.examiner_comment: Overall, students did much better with part b compared to part a. Those who correctly identified the hawk-dove game tended to do quite well. Where they attempted to apply other game theoretic approaches, marks were awarded for relevant concepts.

2023-7-5.examiner_comment: When answering this question many students disregarded the "bottom-up" requirement which meant they initialised the chart with the root node and then produced an inefficient algorithm (often they noticed this by the end and mentioned it in part g). However, the root node initialisation provided a implicit edge ordering for section c) so they then didn't need to specify this explicitly. The question was considered holistically, for instance in part e) it was necessary for the candidate to specify how history was recorded and often this came in part a) or part c) --- they were awarded full marks for e) if the information was available earlier.
topics: Syntax Trees and Tree Adjoining Grammars

2023-7-6.examiner_comment: When answering part a) of the question, I allowed candidates to deviate from exact tree draw in terms of unary rules at the leaves but they were not allowed to change the constituent structure. Candidates were not penalised for lack of linguistic knowledge; they were assessed on knowledge of how formal grammars work, not on the grammar of English which was used as an example. Generally part a) was answered well. In part b) the most consistent errors were not specifying the tree root and not lexicalising the grammar. In part c) the candidates tended to be consistent with their previous answer and most remembered the two operations. However, adjuction was often used incorrectly. Excellent answers provided some evidence of systemicity in the generation. In part d) most spotted the rogue relation but the explanation was often partial or contained incorrect statements that suggested a lack of understanding.
topics: Syntax Trees and Tree Adjoining Grammars
Surface Mesh Topology and Euler Characteristics

2023-7-8.examiner_comment: P7Q8 was only attempted by 10 students and 4 of them attempted to solve only a small subset of the questions, hence the slightly low median.

2023-7-9.examiner_comment: This question invited candidates to consider real benefits of recent advances in LLMs. Application of cognitive dimensions was generally good. Poor answers were those suggesting LLMs might solve problems by further technical advance (or magic), rather than addressing basic usability issues. In part b), most students were distracted by the marketing promise of AI, suggesting that home heating might now be a discretionary or entertainment matter, rather than recognising that the fundamental home automation problem being solved is a very old one (first wave HCI).

2023-7-10.examiner_comment: This question was quite straightforward, and all candidates provided some kind of answer to all elements. I therefore marked strictly, and attended closely to "graphical mark or property." In part b), many candidates referred to a "pie chart" or a "line graph," which is not a mark or a property. I also required precise mechanisms of correspondence in part c), so it was not acceptable to offer commonsense explanations such as a photograph being "literal" or a chart "metaphorical". In cases where a candidate did refer to a whole representation rather than a property, some points were awarded in part c) for places where a property of the representation was mentioned. In part d), a few candidates continue to report that "cognitive walkthrough" is a method for user observation, which is not taught, and incorrect - perhaps a misinterpretation of part 1A interaction design, or a misinformed college supervisor.

2024-4-5.examiner_comment: Part a) many people forgot that not all C++ functions are methods. Part b) many people read 'any value between 8 and 16' as either 8 or 16. Some read 'in a char' to mean a char provided by a caller, rather than an architectural feature. Part d) students should know that writing just 'yes' or 'no' is never sufficient for full marks in the CST. Also, 'give an example' requires an example, preferably coded in C++, so describing the general pattern cannot be awarded full credit. A C-style down cast is not checked at runtime, neither is static_cast.
