2024-4-6.examiner_comment: Part a) since the question spoke of the built-in comparison operator, no credit was awarded relating to user-defined overrides of less than. Part b) separation of definition and implementation is orthogonal to other aspects of object-oriented programming, so no credit was awarded for other aspects such as inheritance. Part d) many answers invoked foo on only the removed item. Also, please don't use malloc in C++ code.

2024-4-7.examiner_comment: A comparatively easy question, where even candidates who clearly lacked a full understanding of the problem were able to earn relatively high marks. There were 65 scripts, yielding a top-heavy histogram with a minimum score of 1 mark, a maximum 20 marks (awarded twice) and a median of 14 marks. The most frequent score was 16 marks, awarded to 9 candidates. For part (a.i), most candidates got full marks, except those few who raised password length to alphabet size instead of vice versa. Part (a.ii), considered trivial because it required re-explaining the material from the lectures without any inventive step, was instead answered rather more poorly than expected, highlighting patchy understanding. It was particularly grating to see several candidates "searching" for a digest by scanning all entries in what was supposed to be a hash table with constant time lookup. Also, quite a few candidates failed to consider the case in which the digest was not found. Part (a.iii), short and easy, was well answered. In part (a.iv) a small minority of students would not venture any numbers. Most sensible numerical estimates were accepted but the line was drawn at implausible scenarios such as recruiting thousands of collaborators, each with a bank of thousands of GPUs. Although this was not required, very few candidates translated their final estimate of (say) 10e11 seconds into a more appropriate time unit such as years or millennia; and even fewer commented on the feasibility of the task. For Part (b), almost all candidates were able to define a collision but the quality of the ensuing commentary varied.

2024-4-8.examiner_comment: A question that clearly distinguished those with hands-on experience of buffer overflow from those who could superficially handwave about it but would not have been capable of exploiting the vulnerability. There were 60 scripts. The minimum was 2 marks, the maximum and most frequent score 20 marks (awarded 8 times) and the median was 13 marks. The question achieved its intended pedagogical goal of highlighting and rewarding those who had acquired the practical ability to carry out the attack. Part (a), trivial, was answered correctly by almost everyone. Most people answered Part (b) correctly, though it was surprising to see a few candidates who answered it incorrectly while still saying in Part (c) that they wanted a longer nop sled (where would it fit then?). Almost everyone answered Part (c) correctly. Parts (d) and (e), instead, showed whether candidates had a clue about what to do in practice, and demonstrated that quite a few didn't. But it was satisfying to witness and reward a good batch of perfect or almost perfect answers.

2024-5-1.examiner_comment: Quite a number of innovative answers.

2024-5-2.examiner_comment: A question focussed upon layer 2; part (a) most confusion resulted from conflating scramblers and block codecs with physical wire representation (eg NRZI/manchester etc). part (b) most students read the question and provided a good interpretation of hidden/exposed nodes problem; this combined with acknolweding BEB and carrier sense, combined with Collision avoidance via CTS/RTS and ACK retured full marks.

2024-5-3.examiner_comment: Ambiguous language in part a and b of the question means there are unintentionally two correct answers for both parts. This has effectively rendered this part of the question of no significant value. All students who did attempted each parts a and b got the three marks due. This effect can be seen in the median mark for this question. I'd suggest a selective correction of (between -1 and -3) might be usefully applied if the effect impacts classing. My apologies, the ambiguiity in my lecture notes only arose in marking.

2024-5-4.examiner_comment: Part b ii) The lectured defintion of a conflicting elemental operations was expected, not the general notion poor transaction management. Part b iv) some candidates read 'composite' as 'atomic', which is understandable given the implication of the question, but full credit was awarded for comparison of the two approaches, regardless of naming. Part b v) bank account credits and debits are increments/decrements and so not allowed as part of the example. Part c) a number of candidates also had locks and shared variables in their answers, but the point of this topic is avoiding mutable shared state, so this received little credit.

2024-5-5.examiner_comment: Most candidates did well on standard results in the first four parts. Range of results for the pseudo-code exercise. Answers to final qustion often focused on trade-offs in failure-free execution, but not impact of attempting to use Lamport timestamps if any node does fail or is slow.

2024-5-6.examiner_comment: Part (b) proved to be rather easy, so I ensured that key details were included in the description of each instruction. For example, for the CONST instruction the immediate comes from the instruction but I also wanted to know that the immedate was zero extended (unsigned) and not sign extended. I was expecting to see higher marks for part (d); I don't know why so many candidates found this 3 mark question so difficult! Around three candidates gave a detailed description of the code in part (c) but failed to include some details of the result produced in part (e), so I gave credit in (e) where the correct answer appeared in their answer for (c).

2024-5-7.examiner_comment: I was surprised that so few students answered this question well, so marking had to be lenient. Most did not fully understand where forwarding paths are added to a pipeline to reduce data hazards. Also, many thought that only conditional branches caused control hazards rather whereas all branches can cause a control hazard. For question (c)(iv), many students failed to remember that on an L1 cache miss you still need to include the L1 cache latency.

2024-5-8.examiner_comment: In part (a) the majority of students correctly explained that one large shared cache would result in high access latency but then failed to apply this argument to part (c) when a large shared TLB (a cache of virtual-to-physical address translations) was proposed, which I find most strange. For part (f), quite a few students used "strict consistency" and then correctly described "sequential consistency". I'm uncertain why this inconsistency has arisen, but decided to give full marks even if the wrong term was used provided the description was correct.

2024-6-7.examiner_comment: For part (a) a lot of students missed box for always. There was no pattern of what they could do better than something else. For part (b) they did the best out of all parts: they seemed to have understood the setup. Those that didn't get part (b) did badly generally. Part (c) was the worst of all, no one got full marks. It is possible that students were optimising their time, since this required a bit of thinking and being careful how they wrote things down. For this, if they had the right idea, they got 3 marks, if they did some steps of reasoning using just rules, then they got 4 marks, if the did some proof steps they got 5 marks and if good poorf steps then 6 marks. They got 2 marks if they had the right formalisation but nothing else, and 1 mark if some correct application of rules with nothing else.

2024-6-8.examiner_comment: In general the students did well. Most of them didn't remember what Kowalski form is. Thus for part aiii they didn't use it but I gave them full marks if the got the right resolution even in clause form. The rest was straightforward. In DPLL a lot of them forgot that there is a step called pure where a literal only appears in one polarity (positive or negative). I deducted the mark, even though they might have found a correct model through other rules.

2024-6-9.examiner_comment: Overall, I thought this question was quite challenging, since it covered so many different topics from the course. The two hardest questions were to work out the subtyping relation in (a), and the proof of transitivity in (d)(ii). Both of these questions required students to apply what they had learned in a new context.

2024-6-10.examiner_comment: The distribution of answers was strongly bimodal in this question: students typically got all of the solution, or struggled with every part of it. I was particularly pleased how many students correctly defined semantic equivalence, because it involved generalizing from the definition in lectures to an entirely new language.

2024-7-1.examiner_comment: In many cases the answers were very good. Solutions closer to the median usually suffered from a combination of one or more of: not setting a useable activation in Part (b); failing to optimize for the width; or not answering the question that was actually asked in Part (c).

2024-7-2.examiner_comment: Generally quite well-completed. Marks were often lost however when candidates went beyond the format imposed by this particular algorithm. For example, by introducing = as a predicate and assuming that the correct semantics would automatically be applied.

2024-7-3.examiner_comment: Overall, the marking scheme worked well. For example, for (a), most students identified the copyright issues with training data, but strong answers also identified the challenges with who owns the output. An even stronger answer discussed how this was still being played out in the courts, and that the law was taking time to catch up with technology.

2024-7-4.examiner_comment: As these are essay-based questions, there are some good answers students provided that were not covered by the example answers. In particular, for (b), students were awarded marks for talking about the role of regulation, and for pointing out that good signals are those that are cheap to emit but expensive to mimic. For (c), some students spoke about the hidden information may be personal information, such as health insurers not having information about those they are insuring.

2024-7-5.examiner_comment: Parts a) and e) on string expresssions were mostly answered correctly. Their purpose was to check the candidates understanding for what followed. Part e) was excepted with e+ or e* either were a possibilty. The candidate was expected to be consistent with their choice in what followed. For part b) Some canidates failed to fully specify the FSA (the same is true of the grammar in Part d) but almost all produced a FSA that matched the expression. The proofs for part c) and f) were fairly poor. Most candidates knew of the pumping lemmas but many failed to produce a convincing proof. Some got the pumping lemma properties wrong for the CFGs. Most candidates were able to find the grammar for part d). Credit was given for realising their were two different things that the grammar had to achieve and further pounts were awarded if the candidate specified those two things correctly.

2024-7-6.examiner_comment: There appear to be two distributions of students attempting this paper. There are a sizable portion of students who appear to have selected this as their last question and have hurriedly attempted to jot something down to try to get one mark for parts of the question (typically they have written the revelant equation but not attempted the maths or attempted the AND part of the questions which required a written explanation). These students account for the majority of the scripts that score between 2 and 8 (there are 8 parts to the question). If these students are removed the median becomes 12. The remaining students have attempted the questions more fully. Every Part of the question had the full range of marks awarded, but unfortunately, no one student managed to achieve the maximum on every Part within one script leading to a top mark of 18. Beyond this answers fall in to several categories: those who have memorised the equations but can't apply to the scenario; those who know the equations, can apply to the basic scenario but are challenged by the extended analysis of the data; those who can do it all but have made small omissions in their explanations. Students performed relatively poorly on part f), many not knowing the equation for channel capacity (or what to do with it). For part h) many students failed to comment on the implications of the LEFT and RIGHT flag positions in the table. Throughout, small mistakes in the maths were not penalised.

2024-7-8.examiner_comment: There are only five students that attempted this question and one (2167E) only attempted to solve part of it, hence the median is not very informative in this case. Inspecting marks for individual parts, there were students correctly solving (a) and (c), whereas (b) was a bit more difficult for the students.
